sections.html:
• Name: Decorator crab
  • Other names: Masking crab, Camposcia decorator crab, Spider decorator crab, Collector crab, Velcro crab, Majoid crab
  • Scientific name: Camposcia retusa
  • Tank size: 10 gallons (about 40 litres)
  • Keeping: Easy
  • Breeding: Very difficult
  • Average size (carapace): 1.5–2 cm (0.6–0.8 inches)
  • Average size (leg span): 8–10 cm (3–4 inches)
  • Optimal temperature: 26–30°C (78–86°F)
  • Water type (specific gravity): 1.021–1.030
  • Optimal pH: 8.1–8.5
  • Optimal KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: Omnivore
  • Temperament (reef safe): Semi-aggressive
  • Life span: up to 5 years
  • Colour form: Reddish-brown

This species is widely distributed across the Indo-West-Pacific region, inhabiting both tropical and subtropical waters.

The Decorator crabs were found near:

  • Philippine Islands
  • Cape Grenville and Port Denison
  • Oshima, Japan
  • India
  • Cocos Island
  • Sri Lanka
  • East and South Africa
  • West and North East Australia
  • eastwards to Samoa and Fiji
  • Mauritius
  • Pakistan
  • Nicobar Islands
  • Christmas Island
  • Indonesia
  • Australia
The Decorator crabs prefer to inhabit muddy and rocky weedy areas of the lower intertidal zone, hiding in and under coral reefs, big boulders, and rocks.
Because of their relatively small size, even nano marine tanks (10 gallons or 40 litres) will be good enough for a crab.

Decorator crabs are low-maintenance and easy to care for. They do not require large tanks and are pretty forgiving when it comes to water conditions. Sometimes you do not even need to buy them, as they are great hitchhikers.

Reef safety: Although these crabs are generally considered safe to keep in reef tanks, there is a possibility that they may occasionally nibble on soft corals, especially if they are hungry or lack food options. Since they are not particularly mobile, they might simply miss the food given to them. Their decorating behaviour may also involve picking up small items from the tank, which could accidentally disturb or damage delicate coral structures. If you still decide to keep them in a reef tank, watch them closely and offer varied foods to help reduce possible harm to corals.

• Temperature: Decorator crabs prefer warm water in a range of 26–30°C (78–86°F). However, they can easily tolerate temperatures down to 22°C (72°F).
  • pH: Maintain optimal pH values of 8.1–8.5.
  • Hardness: Keep water hardness values between 8–12 dKH.
  • SG: They can tolerate specific gravity in the range between 1.021 and 1.030. However, the ideal range is 1.0264–1.0279 (35–37 ppt).
  • Calcium and magnesium: Keeping calcium concentration in the range of 400 to 450 ppm and magnesium between 1,250 and 1,350 ppm is optimal.

Lighting: Since these crabs are nocturnal animals, they do not really need much light. In their natural habitats, they tend to live in areas that are protected from sunlight such as coral reefs, rockpools, seagrass leaves, etc. If you keep corals and fish in the tank, the lighting should be adapted to their needs.

Filtration: There are no special requirements. As long as you have a filter that works well with the size of your tank, you will be fine.

Substrate: There are no special requirements either.

Decorations: The aim of incorporating decor in an aquarium is to replicate the natural habitat and provide enough hiding places. Additionally, they naturally use materials to camouflage themselves. Therefore, providing decorations and hiding spots mimics their natural habitat, reducing stress and promoting their well-being in the tank.

These crabs are classified as opportunistic omnivores. In their natural environment, they eat carrion, small sea stars, mollusks, worms, algae, and ascidians (sea squirts), all slow-moving or stationary organisms.

In aquariums, the Decorator crabs will eat anything extra in the tank. This may include leftover meaty foods, detritus, and/or the algae that grow naturally in the tank.

Foods the Decorator crabs will enjoy, for example:

  • small pieces of shrimp
  • chopped prawn and mussels
  • frozen bloodworms

Uneaten food was removed the following morning.

How often to feed: Adults can be fed 3–4 times a week whereas juveniles should be fed daily. The most important rule is not to let them starve. Otherwise, despite their relatively peaceful temper, they can become unpredictable or aggressive.

  • Diet type: Mostly carnivore/omnivore
  • Food preference: Meat
  • Feeding frequency: 3–4 times a week

These crabs exhibit decorating behaviour, which has made them popular in the aquarium hobby. However, this behaviour is not constant: they don't continuously change their appearance. Once decorated, they will add new decorations at a slower pace than initially.

Decorator crabs are nocturnal and will spend most of their days hidden from the light. At night they roam around the tank looking for food or a new hiding spot.

These crabs are very slow-moving. They prefer crawling over climbing and typically avoid climbing whenever possible, possibly because they carry extra weight on their bodies, making them less agile and slower.

Why do they decorate themselves? According to the study, decorating in this species appears to function primarily as an antipredator response, with crabs decorating at higher rates when access to shelter is limited. However, it is still unknown how they choose their decorations. Experiments showed that the way Camposcia retusa decorates itself doesn't help it blend in with its surroundings.

Decorator crabs mostly decorate themselves with sponges, algae, and detritus, mostly on their shell and back legs, which might be because of their body shape. They use their claws to grab materials around them, move these materials to their mouthparts where they roughen the edges, and finally attach them to their bodies. Decorations stick to the crab's body with small, velcro-like hairs (setae); the ones used for decorating have hooks to keep the decorations in place. Even as they grow bigger, they keep decorating themselves just as much.

Interesting fact: of the 900 species within this superfamily, at least 75% are estimated to decorate to some degree.

  • Social: No
  • Active: No
  • Aggression: Semi-aggressive
  • Burrowers: No

Sexing Camposcia retusa is extremely difficult and will likely be very challenging for ordinary aquarists. Scientific literature indicates that sexual dimorphism starts to appear at the C5 (molt) stage:

  • Females develop 4 pairs of pleopods on the 2nd to 5th somites of the pleon, while males have only 2.
  • In males, the first pair of pleopods grows longer as they mature, with longitudinal groove setae appearing at the C8 stage.
  • The second pair of pleopods shows minimal growth from C8 to C10, and no setae are observed up to the C10 stage.

Despite its popularity in the aquarium trade, there have been no documented instances of successful larval cultivation of these crabs. Currently, the pet industry depends on wild-caught animals. Factors such as water quality, temperature, and the availability of suitable food sources are crucial. In scientific literature, there are two studies on this issue; one of them describes a detailed procedure for a reliable larval culture protocol for Camposcia retusa.

Maturity

On average, the development time from C1 to C10 (fully grown animal) is about 7 months.

Fecundity

Decorator crabs are not very prolific. They generally have several dozen eggs. The eggs are incubated in the chamber limited by the sternum and abdomen, and the hatchlings remain under the female's abdomen for a certain period before dispersing.

Incubation and hatching

Incubation generally lasts around 1 month. The eggs hatch into miniature versions of the adult. It was found that egg incubation generally takes between 21–25 days under the following conditions:

  • Water temperature 26.7–28.9°C (80–84°F)
  • Salinity 1.0264–1.0279 (35–37 ppt)
  • Photoperiod L:D = 14:10 hours
  • pH 7.9–8.2
  • NH4+/NH3 and NO2 < 0.25 ppm
  • NO3 < 5.0 ppm

Note: At salinity 26–32 ppt, all larvae died within 3 days. Zoeal survival was significantly higher at salinity 35 and 38 ppt. Culture salinity should be kept between 35–37 ppt for zoeal larvae, then reduced to 30–33 ppt at the megalopa stage.

Hatching of larvae

Larvae normally hatch overnight, and occasionally in the early morning. On the morning of hatching, aeration was first stopped, then the room light was turned off, and a torch was directed to an upper corner of the tank to attract the positively phototactic larvae. The larvae gathered were then gently scooped with a small beaker with as little water as possible.

Larval feeding

Food is arguably the most important factor affecting the success of larval culture of marine crabs. Prey size should be suitable for easy consumption by larval mouthparts. Experiments showed that newly hatched Artemia nauplii at a density of 10 individuals per millilitre seem sufficient for Camposcia retusa larvae. Larvae fed with rotifers did not survive. Lowering stocking density during the megalopa stage may reduce cannibalism among megalopae.

Etymology: No specific etymological source for "Camposcia" was found beyond its common usage for this species. It is plausible that the genus name originates from the Latin word "campus", meaning "field" or "plain", which could indicate a connection to the habitats where these crabs are typically found. The species name "retusa" comes from the Latin "retusus", meaning "blunted or rounded off", possibly describing a characteristic of the crab's body shape or features.

Description: Adults typically grow to about 1.5–2 cm in carapace width and around 8–10 cm across the leg span. Many articles mention that they can grow up to 3 cm in carapace width, but this is an exception. Their appearance varies substantially in shape and colour depending on what they use for decoration.

  • Carapace: Pear-shaped, longer than wide, with a bumpy surface covered with curly hair. Parts of the body around the stomach area are slightly swollen.
  • Abdomen: Wide and round, with six sections in both males and females.
  • Rostrum: The head is broad, slightly deflexed anteriorly, with an emarginated anterior edge. The parts near the mouth are also hairy.
  • Setae: Curled or hooked setae (small hair-like structures) all over the body.
  • Eyes: Protruding and able to move sideways, with a small blunt spine near each eye. The eyestalks are long and slender.
  • Antennae: A long, slender base with shorter segments covered in tiny hairs.
  • Claws: Thin, short and covered in soft hairs, with small teeth on the inner edges that fit together.
  • Legs: The walking legs are elongated and covered in thick hair. The second leg is shorter than the others, and they gradually lengthen from the third leg. The last leg is as long as the third. Total length is about 3 to 5 times the carapace length.
  • Colour: Usually reddish-brown, with the back of the claws reddish-white.

Taxonomy: Kingdom Animalia; Phylum Arthropoda; Subphylum Crustacea; Class Malacostraca; Order Decapoda; Superfamily Majidae (spider crabs); Genus Camposcia.

Lifespan: There is no data on maximum lifespan in the wild. In captivity, these crabs can live up to 3–5 years if appropriately cared for.

Conclusion: The Decorator crab is commonly found in hobby aquariums due to its ability to live in captivity. As with other majoid crabs, they decorate their carapaces and legs with items found on the reef floor, including sponges, corals, rubble, etc. They are very easy to care for and require minimal attention. However, if you want a crab that actively crawls both day and night, they may not be suitable. Keeping them in a reef aquarium can also be problematic for corals.
